section_summary: This section documents U.S., British, Dutch, and other Allied efforts to monitor and restrict Japan’s access to strategic commodities, including scrap iron, petroleum, nickel, Manila hemp, copra cake, and Latin American minerals. It contains memoranda, diplomatic correspondence, shipping intelligence, and statistical tables concerning suspected export-control evasion and Japan’s wartime resource position. Later documents address public and congressional criticism of prewar American exports to Japan and provide official explanations of the 1940 scrap-iron licensing restrictions.

subfiles.title: Continuation of letter on the North American Syndicate diesel-oil scheme
subfiles.to: Jacques J. Reinstein, Department of State
subfiles.about: Provides additional Hong Kong information on a scheme to move diesel oil from Mexico to Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: The concluding page reports that the North American Syndicate’s Shanghai branch was trying to import diesel oil and remit money to Los Angeles through black-market channels. R. S. Boyd had begun arrangements through banks in Shanghai and Mexico City. Dent urges prompt action in Mexico or California and sends copies to Thornburg, Yost, and the Rockefeller Committee.

subfiles.title: Reported Illegal Shipment of Scrap Iron to Japan
subfiles.from: Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Investigates statistics suggesting that scrap iron was exported to Japan after the governing license had been revoked.
subfiles.summary: Export Control statistics showed 331,520 pounds of scrap shipped through Port Huron under license FA-49 after licenses for Japan had been revoked. The Port Huron collector denied having a record of the exports, while John Miles supplied photostats of the collector’s reports supporting the statistics. Miles intended to refer the discrepancy to Monroe Oppenheimer of the Economic Defense Board.

subfiles.title: Reported Illegal Shipment of Scrap Iron to Japan—copy 1
subfiles.from: Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the memorandum investigating a disputed post-revocation scrap shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the report that scrap exports cleared Port Huron under revoked license FA-49. It records the conflict between the collector’s denial and the photostatic reports supplied by John Miles, as well as the planned referral to the Economic Defense Board.

subfiles.title: Reported Illegal Shipment of Scrap Iron to Japan—copy 2
subfiles.from: Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Second duplicate copy of the memorandum on disputed scrap exports under license FA-49.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that Nissho Company’s license had been revoked and returned through the New Orleans customs collector. Despite Port Huron’s denial, Export Control records indicated that a shipment had cleared there in early January 1941. The matter was to be examined by Economic Defense Board counsel.

subfiles.title: Reported Illegal Shipment of Scrap Iron to Japan—copy 3
subfiles.from: Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Third duplicate copy concerning potentially illegal scrap shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This copy reproduces the export statistics, license history, and contradictory Port Huron customs evidence. It notes that responsibility for yellow licenses had been transferred to the Economic Defense Board before a further explanation could be requested.

subfiles.title: Reported Illegal Shipment of Scrap Iron to Japan—copy 4
subfiles.from: Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Fourth duplicate copy of the report on scrap exports allegedly made after license revocation.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum again identifies 331,520 pounds of scrap reportedly exported through Port Huron under license FA-49. It describes the collector’s denial, John Miles’s rebuttal evidence, and his intended referral of the case to Monroe Oppenheimer.

subfiles.title: British Embassy warning about copra-cake shipment to Japan
subfiles.to: Charles W. Yost, Office of Export Control
subfiles.about: Warns that Madrigal and Company planned to ship 2,000 tons of copra cake from Manila to Japan.
subfiles.summary: London suspected that the copra cake might have an unusually high oil content intended for further pressing in oil-short Japan. Dent asks that the shipment aboard the Konone Maru be stopped or that the cake’s fat content be checked. He suggests treating abnormally rich cake as coconut oil subject to control.

subfiles.title: Handwritten note on possible copra-cake restrictions
subfiles.about: Records a brief, partly illegible discussion of shortages and possible restrictions on exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note appears to consider whether an oil shortage in Japan justified stopping or restricting the relevant exports. It also refers to London’s recommendation, but much of the handwriting is illegible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Exports of Copra Cake to Japan
subfiles.to: Division of Exports and Defense Aid
subfiles.about: Assesses Philippine copra-cake trade and the British proposal to control shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews normal Philippine copra-cake exports and their wartime collapse as European and American shipping became unavailable. Philippine Affairs preferred analyzing Japan-bound cake and licensing it only when an abnormally high fat content made it equivalent to copra or coconut oil. It did not object if policymakers wished to prohibit cake intended for cattle feed or fertilizer, though doing so could reduce mill and producer revenues.

subfiles.title: Request for policy advice on licensing copra cake
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Division of Exports and Defense Aid
subfiles.about: Asks whether copra cake should be added to the export-licensing list.
subfiles.summary: Yost notes that the commodity reported by the British Embassy as moving from the Philippines to Japan was not subject to licensing. He asks whether the Economic Defense Board should be requested to place it under control.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding evidence of down-grading Manila fiber
subfiles.from: George C. McGhee, Office of Production Management
subfiles.to: Thomas K. Finletter, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards evidence that high-grade Manila fiber may have reached Japan after being falsely graded as lower-quality material.
subfiles.summary: McGhee reports that Colonel Chickering confirmed leakage of good fiber to Japan through the practice of sweetening lower-grade purchases. Chickering believed the problem would be difficult to stop unless the United States also bought some poorer grades. McGhee asks whether preclusive purchasing or stronger export controls would be the better remedy.

subfiles.title: Manila Fiber Statistics
subfiles.about: Presents statistical evidence concerning possible misbranding of high-grade Manila fiber exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes a sharp late-August increase in shipments to Japan and suspects that Japanese shippers may have labeled high-grade fiber as low grade. Tables show stripped and decorticated Manila-fiber exports and 1940 abaca production by district. The production table emphasizes the large share of cordage-grade fiber produced around Davao in Mindanao, where Japanese interests were prominent.

subfiles.title: Office of Philippine Affairs comments on abaca exports to Japan
subfiles.to: Thomas K. Finletter and Department of State officials
subfiles.about: Evaluates whether recent abaca exports and alleged down-grading required a change in export policy.
subfiles.summary: Philippine Affairs found no alarming trend in the August figures and expected shipments to decline because Japanese vessels had largely stopped calling after frozen-fund controls. It explains the quota for low Y or W grades, Japan’s normal annual purchases, and abaca’s importance to the Japanese fishing industry. The office recommends asking the High Commissioner and Fiber Inspection Board to investigate down-grading but sees no need to alter the directive unless the purpose is to exert additional pressure on Japan.

subfiles.title: Request for advice on replying about Manila-fiber leakage
subfiles.about: Requests recommendations on whether all hemp exports to Japan should be prohibited.
subfiles.summary: Finletter recalls that low YOTW grades had been allowed to go to Japan because they were believed to lack military utility. Later telegrams made him question that decision. He asks whether prohibiting all grades would now be necessary to achieve the intended restriction.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Netherlands comments on deliveries to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a letter containing Netherlands Government comments on deliveries of materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references the original Netherlands Legation letter and its memorandum to confidential file 751g.94/404-2/3. It identifies the subject as delivery of certain materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: Request for a proposed answer to British hemp letters
subfiles.about: Asks what response should be made to John S. Dent’s letters concerning Manila-hemp exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost forwards the British Embassy correspondence and requests guidance on an answer. The issue is whether further shipments of Manila hemp, including waste grades, should be prevented.

subfiles.title: British confirmation of Japanese hemp shipments from the Philippines
subfiles.to: Charles W. Yost, Office of Export Control
subfiles.about: Confirms September hemp shipments from Davao and Cebu to Japan and presses for restrictions on waste hemp.
subfiles.summary: Dent reports that the Kasima Maru left Davao with 9,993 bales and the Tai Maru left Cebu with 25,000 bales, mainly for Kobe. The information corrected an earlier State Department belief that the reported sailing was mistaken. Dent asks whether steps can be taken to stop further Japanese purchases of Philippine waste hemp.

subfiles.title: British request to prohibit waste-hemp exports to Japan
subfiles.to: Charles W. Yost, Office of Export Control
subfiles.about: Explains the Japanese uses of waste hemp and asks about the Philippine export quota.
subfiles.summary: London reported that Japan sorted waste hemp, using sound fibers for rope and damaged fibers for paper. Dent asks the United States to prohibit further Philippine exports, noting that comparable Empire commodities such as Indian coir had already been stopped. He also requests information on the status of the 16-million-pound quota and the reported Matai Maru shipment.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Dutch Export Control Policy
subfiles.about: Sets out Netherlands East Indies policy for restricting strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Van Mook traces the shift from prewar trade concerns to restrictions on strategic materials after Germany’s advances and Japan’s move into French Indochina. He calls for coordinated Allied controls designed to lower Japan’s war potential without deliberately starving the population. The recommended policy was a complete embargo on oil, rubber, metals, ores, and similar war materials; small exports of fibers, copra, and kapok; and normal exports of commodities such as sugar, coffee, maize, and timber.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to petroleum-shipment correspondence
subfiles.about: References correspondence and clippings concerning petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a letter from Senator Francis Maloney with enclosures from Thomas Fish and two newspaper clippings. The original material was filed under petroleum file 852.24/999.

subfiles.title: Shipments of Bolivian Minerals to Japan in November 1941
subfiles.from: Allan Dawson, American Legation, La Paz
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese-bound shipments of Bolivian minerals through Chilean ports in November 1941.
subfiles.summary: The despatch lists copper, antimony, tungsten, lead-silver, asbestos, and cobalt carried by Japanese vessels from Arica and Antofagasta to Osaka, Kobe, and Yokohama. Banco Minero manager Santiago Schulze maintained that the final tungsten and antimony had left Bolivia before the outbreak of war and that later balances were not shipped. Dawson adds that Banco Minero urgently needed United States markets for copper and antimony formerly sold to Japan.

subfiles.title: Note on Japanese iron supplies from Manchuria
subfiles.about: Records an estimate that Manchurian production might soon meet Japan’s wartime iron and steel needs.
subfiles.summary: The note recalls an American businessman’s statement to Military Intelligence that Japan would soon obtain enough iron and steel products from Manchuria to supply its war requirements. It was filed in connection with Herbert Feis’s work on Japanese iron sources.

subfiles.title: Japanese dependence on Manchurian industrial plants
subfiles.about: Calls attention to Japanese reliance on industrial facilities in Manchuria when planning future operations in China.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies Manchurian steel plants, iron-ore extraction works, and synthetic-oil factories as vital Japanese assets. It suggests that Military Intelligence possessed detailed information on their locations.

subfiles.title: Mitsui inquiry for nickel
subfiles.about: Reports a Mitsui approach to the International Nickel Company for a substantial quantity of nickel.
subfiles.summary: Feis states that Mitsui representatives approached Mr. Suhle to ask whether nickel could be obtained. They reportedly hoped the proposed discussions with Japanese envoy Kurusu might make the transaction possible.

subfiles.title: Shipment of strategic metals from the Antofagasta district to Japan
subfiles.from: W. R. Gaines, U.S. naval intelligence reporting from Peru
subfiles.to: Office of the Chief of Naval Intelligence and Department of State
subfiles.about: Details strategic cargoes loaded aboard Japanese steamers at Peruvian and Chilean ports.
subfiles.summary: The report itemizes copper, lead, antimony, manganese, tungsten, vanadium, asbestos, mercury, cotton, and other cargoes carried by the Norfolk Maru, Bakito Maru, and Terukawa Maru. It identifies consignors, consignees, destination ports, loading ports, and tonnages. A final summary gives strategic-material exports from Callao during September and early October 1941.

subfiles.title: Strategic-material shipments aboard the Azuma Maru
subfiles.to: Office of the Chief of Naval Intelligence and Department of State
subfiles.about: Lists cargo loaded for Japan during the latter part of October 1941.
subfiles.summary: The Azuma Maru loaded antimony, wolfram, quinine, nitrate, potash, and cotton at Arica, Iquique, and Callao. The report states that the vessel sailed directly from Callao for Yokohama on October 30.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on Japanese shortages and poor workmanship
subfiles.about: References a letter reporting shortages, graft, and poorly inspected workmanship in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to the original letter in file 740.0011 P.W./1593. Its subject combines Japanese shortages of food and supplies with reports of graft and defective workmanship.

subfiles.title: British report on Argentine exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Supplies comparative figures for Argentine vanadium, mica, and borax shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Marris reports sharp increases in vanadium and mica exports during the first ten months of 1941 compared with 1940 and 1939. He also notes rising borax shipments, even though borax was apparently outside American negotiations with Argentina.

subfiles.title: Restricted message on Japanese gas grenades
subfiles.to: War Department and Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports technical information obtained from notes and captured examples of Japanese chemical-incendiary grenades.
subfiles.summary: The message describes a one-pint glass grenade containing hydrochloric-acid-related liquid and intended for enclosed spaces such as tanks. British and Near Eastern investigators disagreed over whether the sediment was phosphoric acid used as a stabilizer or phosphorus serving as an incendiary agent. Chemical Warfare Service tests were continuing.

subfiles.title: British report on Japanese barter arrangements with Chile
subfiles.about: Reports Mitsubishi efforts to establish barter or compensating trade between Japan and Chile.
subfiles.summary: The partly garbled letter describes communications between Mitsubishi offices concerning Japanese imports and future purchases of Chilean goods. It discusses deposits or guarantees intended to balance Japanese goods imported into Chile with Chilean exports of corresponding value. Marris forwards the information as evidence of Japanese attempts to build barter trade with Chile.

subfiles.title: British warning about a Mexican diesel-oil transaction
subfiles.to: Jacques J. Reinstein, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports that a scheme to send Mexican diesel oil to the North American Syndicate in Shanghai was nearing completion.
subfiles.summary: Mitsubishi San Francisco had reported an inquiry for 10,000 tons of diesel oil under a Tampico-to-Shanghai bill of lading associated with the Mexican Government. Dent links the scheme to Petróleos León and Abraham Z. Phillips and reports black-market remittances through Los Angeles. Hong Kong information identifies R. S. Boyd as the syndicate’s founder and describes banking arrangements in Shanghai and Mexico City; Dent urges rapid preventive action.

subfiles.title: Internal note on investigating the diesel-oil transaction
subfiles.about: Considers possible methods of investigating or stopping the suspected Mexican diesel-oil transaction.
subfiles.summary: The difficult handwriting indicates that an officer had been consulted but could provide little additional information. The note suggests approaching persons connected with the transaction or asking the Embassy in Mexico to investigate. A final annotation states that, in view of a cable and recent events, the matter appeared moot.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting cancellation of the oil deal
subfiles.about: Reports payments from funds connected with the American Petroleum Export Corporation and cancellation of the oil transaction.
subfiles.summary: Banco Nacional de México had instructions originating through Shanghai banking channels to make payments in New York while a much larger peso balance remained without instructions. The bank said the oil deal had been canceled and the funds released by the American Petroleum Export Corporation to the North American Syndicate.

subfiles.title: Disposal of Strategic Materials Held by Japanese Firms in Brazil
subfiles.from: John F. Simmons, American Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese firms were liquidating stocks of strategic materials in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Japanese companies were selling castor beans, monazite sand, mica, and quartz crystal rather than attempting to deliver them to Japan. Simmons interprets this as evidence that the firms did not expect near-term shipment to Japan. Bank of Brazil freezing controls had immobilized their cash, and the Embassy verified three cases in which companies demanded cash to obtain more liquid assets.

subfiles.title: Referral of inquiry on the end of scrap sales to Japan
subfiles.from: Harriet Root, United States Information Service
subfiles.to: E. Wilder Spaulding, Department of State
subfiles.about: Refers Hoy Garrison’s request for the date on which the United States stopped selling scrap to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Office of Government Reports forwards the citizen’s inquiry to the State Department’s Division of Research and Publications. The form notes that the writer had been informed of the referral.

subfiles.title: Reply to Hoy Garrison on scrap-export prohibition
subfiles.about: States when the United States prohibited scrap-iron and steel exports to destinations including Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that exports of scrap iron and steel outside Great Britain and the Western Hemisphere were prohibited beginning October 15, 1940. The letter directly answers Garrison’s January inquiry.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Japanese petroleum reserves
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Transmits source reporting on Japanese petroleum stocks and the resource motives behind Japanese offensives.
subfiles.summary: A confidential source estimated that Japan held enough petroleum for eighteen to twenty-four months of all-out war and reported a transfer of gasoline and lubricants to Korea. The source claimed that Japanese planners coveted petroleum stocks in the Philippines and expected captured supplies to supplement their reserves. They also believed Dutch East Indies refineries and wells could be restored within two years.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal of Japanese industrial information
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Forwards an enclosed memorandum containing Japanese industrial information.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends Berle a February 14 memorandum received from an outside source. Copies were also directed to Rear Admiral Wilkinson and Brigadier General Raymond E. Lee for naval and military intelligence use.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese iron and steel capacity
subfiles.to: Federal Bureau of Investigation and intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese steel-mill expansion, raw-material imports, scrap stocks, and estimated 1941 output.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says Japanese steel-mill expansion stopped in 1939 when foreign machinery became unavailable, after which domestic equipment allowed continuous operation. It gives figures for scrap and iron-ore imports and lists late-1941 scrap stocks by major company and mill. A detailed table estimates pig-iron and steel-billet production, while noting that actual 1941 output may have been higher.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of Cornelius Walker’s inquiry
subfiles.from: Joseph H. Ball, United States Senate
subfiles.about: Refers a constituent letter seeking information on scrap shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Ball sends Cornelius Walker’s letter to the State Department for consideration and a report. The enclosure concerns both a congressional report and the date on which scrap exports to Japan were stopped.

subfiles.title: Cornelius Walker’s inquiry on scrap exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks for a Dies Committee report and information on the timing of federal orders stopping scrap shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Walker requests a copy of a lengthy Dies Committee report mentioned by Congressman Elliott. He also asks when the government ordered commercial interests to stop sending scrap iron and similar material to Japan, citing a local discussion that the United States had supplied nearly 58 percent of Japan’s imported scrap.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Ball concerning scrap-export controls
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the legal and administrative steps by which scrap exports were brought under control in 1940.
subfiles.summary: Welles states that the July 2, 1940 defense act authorized export controls and that a July 25 proclamation placed No. 1 heavy melting scrap under licensing. Existing licenses were revoked on October 15, and all iron and steel scrap was subsequently restricted to the Western Hemisphere and Great Britain. Four press releases are enclosed for use in answering Walker.

subfiles.title: “Roosevelt Hints Oil Curb on Japan”
subfiles.about: Reports Roosevelt’s explanation for allowing oil exports to Japan and the administration’s response to Japanese expansion in Indochina.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt argued that continued oil shipments had helped postpone Japanese movement into the Dutch East Indies and kept war out of the South Pacific while Britain’s position remained precarious. The article also reports Sumner Welles’s condemnation of Japanese expansion by force and the threat posed to the Philippines, Singapore, and regional trade routes. It discusses possible economic restrictions following Japan’s advance into Indochina.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to Willie H. Germany
subfiles.about: Directs an inquirer to Roosevelt’s July 1941 public explanation of prewar oil policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: The draft acknowledges Germany’s question about scrap iron, gasoline, and oil sales. It cites Roosevelt’s July 24, 1941 remarks to the Volunteer Participation Committee and recommends consulting the July 25 New York Times article titled “Roosevelt Hints Oil Curb on Japan.” The following page contains a brief true-copy or filing annotation.

subfiles.title: Willie Germany’s inquiry about sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks who was chiefly responsible for continuing sales of scrap iron, gasoline, and oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Germany says there had been an almost universal demand that the sales cease. He requests an explanation of responsibility for their continuation.

subfiles.title: Congressman Thom’s request concerning scrap-metal exports
subfiles.from: William R. Thom, House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Requests information to answer a constituent who blamed past exports for a current scrap shortage in Ohio.
subfiles.summary: Thom quotes John D. Cathon’s complaint that sixteen local steel furnaces were idle for lack of scrap and that the United States had been depleted by years of foreign buying. Cathon recalled rapid Japanese loading of scrap on the Pacific Coast in 1933 and accused the government of failing to curtail exports. Thom asks Hull for facts that would permit an informed reply.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Congressman Thom
subfiles.about: Explains the scale of prewar scrap exports and the legal basis for the 1940 restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that scrap exports became substantial after 1933 but never exceeded roughly six to eight percent of total domestic consumption in any year. Earlier proposals to restrict them lacked a sufficient policy or legal basis, and general export-control authority did not exist until July 2, 1940. The administration then placed heavy melting scrap under license from August 1, extended controls to all grades in October, and limited authorized destinations to Great Britain and the Western Hemisphere.
